tasks.task_description: Task 1: Build a Human Capital network model of ICM's personnel situation from the supplied table1.csv, stating the model and its assumptions. Deliverable is a reproducible model of the 370-position organization across its 7 position levels.
tasks.task_analysis: The data is a per-level summary (7 levels, 370 positions) with no individual or tie data, so the 'network' is represented at the level (layer) granularity that the data actually supports. The organizational graph (Figure 1 in the problem) is a hierarchy of 7 levels; churn and information flow propagate along the level-adjacency (an employee's peers and direct reports/bosses). Data cleaning: the raw CSV is not valid UTF-8; the Greek sigma is stored as the two bytes 0xA6 0xD2 (a CP1252-era artifact), which a naive decode turns into U+FFFD. I decoded with replacement, then mapped each corrupted glyph back to sigma (unambiguous, since sigma is the only non-ASCII glyph in the sheet). The experienced-employee salary cell was a bare sigma in the original; Expert Exchange 1 confirmed the company median sigma equals experienced-worker pay, so that cell is 1.0 sigma. Repaired rows: total positions verified = 370. All monetary quantities are expressed in units of sigma (company median income), matching the problem's convention that decisions are made in relative sigma rather than exact dollars. Level adjacency: a level's neighbours are the level one above and one below plus its own tier (peers).
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Let i index levels 0..6 (0=Inexperienced employee ... 6=Senior manager/Executive). State per level: F_i(t) filled, V_i(t) vacant, capacity C_i (fixed, from data: C = [150,110,30,25,25,20,10], total 370). Pay s_i (sigma/yr): [0.9,1.0,0.9,1.5,2.0,4.0,8.0]; training t_i (sigma/yr): [0.3,0.1,0.05,0.3,0.2,0.6,0.5]; recruitment cost r_i (sigma): [0.1,0.3,0.3,0.6,0.6,0.7,1.2]; median time-to-recruit L_i (months): [1,3,2,4,5,6,7]. Model is a monthly Euler system (step = 1 month). Churn is a diffusive SIS-like process on the level network: baseline quit rate q_i (per year) plus a contagion term driven by the recent-churner fraction among a level's neighbours (Exchange 1: churn diffuses through ties). q_i = base_i + kappa * frac_i, where frac_i is the fill-weighted fraction of recent churners over level i and its two adjacent levels, and kappa = 0.5/yr. Monthly quits = (q_i/12)*F_i. Hiring: a company-wide external-hiring cap H = 78 net-new headcount/yr (calibrated so the observed 18% churn is balanced at the current 85% fill; Exchange 2: external throughput ~30-37 plus internal promotions), allocated across levels proportional to their shortfall from the 85% fill target. Each external hire enters a per-level pipeline and arrives after L_i months (Exchange 2 lead-time constraint). Internal promotions move an existing person up one level (no net headcount) into mid/senior vacancies, capped by a qualified-subordinate pool (12% of the level below). Initial state: F_i = 0.85*C_i, with the pipeline pre-seeded by the in-flight hires consistent with the steady state. sigma rises 2%/yr (inflation).
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: The model reproduces the observed steady state: starting at 85% filled with 18% churn (36% at middle managers, 2x the company average as the problem states), the fill ratio holds at 86.6% after 2 years and sustains the 80% floor. This is the anchor the other tasks perturb. Limitations: the level aggregation loses individual heterogeneity and the actual tie topology of Figure 1; the contagion coefficient kappa is an assumption, not measured, and the model is deterministic (no stochastic individual-level variability). The 85% is treated as the current equilibrium per the problem statement, so absolute churn is not independently validated against the data.

tasks.task_description: Task 2: Identify and incorporate the dynamic processes in the Human Capital network: (1) organizational churn (influence, dissatisfaction) and (2) the direct and indirect effects on organizational productivity.
tasks.task_analysis: Two coupled dynamics are modeled. (1) Churn as a contagion: a worker is more likely to leave if connected former employees have churned (problem issue 2), so churn is an epidemic-like process on the level network rather than independent Poisson quits. The 'recent churner' memory (6-month window) encodes that seeing peers leave raises the quit propensity. Dissatisfaction/being 'stuck' at middle management (problem issue 4) is encoded as the elevated 2x baseline churn at Junior manager and the two supervisor levels. (2) Productivity responds to (a) how many positions are filled and (b) how experienced the incumbents are. Exchange 3 supplied the decision-relevant threshold: below ~90-92% filled, managers feel real operational pain, so productivity is full above a 92% fill ratio and degrades linearly (slope 0.5 per unit fill) below it. New hires have a 24-month experience ramp that imposes a 15% productivity drag while ramping, so a churn surge has a lagged, integrating productivity cost even if headcount is quickly replaced.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Churn dynamics: frac_i(t) = sum_j (R_j(t)*F_j(t)) / sum_j F_j(t) over j in {i, i-1, i+1} (fill-weighted recent-churner fraction among self and adjacent levels). q_i(t) = base_i + kappa*frac_i(t). dF_i = -(q_i/12)F_i + hires_i - promos_out_i + promos_in_i. Recent-churner state R_i decays by (1 - 1/6) per month and is replenished by that month's quit fraction. Productivity: P_i(t) = P0 * [P0 - 0.15*New_i(t)] where New_i is the ramping-hire fraction (decays by 1/24 per month), minus a pain term 0.5*max(0, 0.92 - fill_ratio(t)) applied when the company-wide fill ratio is below 92%. Aggregate productivity = sum over levels of P_i*(F_i/C_i). The direct effect of churn is the lost filled positions; the indirect effects are (i) the experience-ramp drag on replacement hires and (ii) the below-92% pain penalty, both of which persist after headcount is restored.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: The model shows churn is self-reinforcing in the short run: a quit raises frac_i, which raises q for the next month, so a surge propagates through adjacent levels for a few months before the recent-churner memory decays. Productivity has a hysteresis: even when fill is restored, the experience ramp keeps output depressed for ~2 years after a large replacement wave. Baseline (18% churn) aggregate productivity is ~6.05 (index, sum over levels of fill x quality). Limitations: the contagion is a mean-field over level neighbours, not a true individual-level SIS on the tie graph; the 92% pain threshold and 0.5 slope are planning-level estimates from Exchange 3, and the model treats productivity as proportional to fill rather than capturing task-specific bottlenecks.

tasks.task_description: Task 3: Use the model to analyze ICM's budget requirements for talent management, in units of sigma, for both recruiting and training over the next 2 years.
tasks.task_analysis: Talent-management budget = recruitment cost + training cost (salary is the recurring operating cost and is reported separately for completeness). At the baseline 18% churn, the model runs a 24-month simulation and accumulates per-level recruitment spend (hires x r_i, incurred when a hire is initiated) and per-level training spend (filled x t_i per month, incurred while the position is occupied). All values are in sigma; sigma itself rises 2%/yr so later-year costs are in a slightly higher sigma, but the problem's convention is to report in relative sigma.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Recruitment: R(t) = sum_i (external_hires_i(t) * r_i) accumulated over months, r_i in sigma per hire. Training: T(t) = sum_i (F_i(t) * t_i * (1/12)) per month, t_i in sigma/yr. Salary (for reference): S(t) = sum_i (F_i(t) * s_i * (1/12)). 2-year totals are the sums of the monthly accruals.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Baseline 2-year budget: recruitment ~34.4 sigma, training ~153.3 sigma (total talent-management ~187.7 sigma); salary for reference ~934.4 sigma. Training dominates the recurring talent-management cost because it is assessed on the whole occupied workforce every year, while recruitment is a one-time cost per replacement. Recruiting cost is low in sigma because per-hire costs are 0.1-1.2 sigma. The budget is sensitive to churn: at 25% churn recruitment rises to ~34.8 and training to ~150.7 (2-yr total ~185.5); at 35% churn it is ~35.9 + ~140.7 (2-yr ~176.6) — the training cost falls slightly because fewer positions are occupied, but the real cost is the lost productivity, not the line-item budget. Limitations: sigma is a moving target (2%/yr inflation) so dollar figures would drift; the model does not include one-time transition costs or the opportunity cost of unfilled capacity in the line-item budget.

tasks.task_description: Task 4: Can ICM sustain its 80% full status if the annual churn rate for all positions goes to 25%? How about 35%? What are the costs of these higher turnover rates, and the indirect effects?
tasks.task_analysis: The model is perturbed by setting every level's baseline churn to 25% (and 35%) while keeping the same hiring cap, lead times, and promotion rules. 'Sustain 80%' means the fill ratio never drops below 0.80 over the 2-year horizon. Exchange 3 framed 80% as a staffing-crisis level (well below the healthy mid-90s), so the answer reports both the raw 80% threshold and the quality-of-staffing picture.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Run the monthly system with base_i = 0.25 for all i (scenario churn25) and base_i = 0.35 for all i (scenario churn35). Track fill_ratio(t) = sum_i F_i / 370 and record the minimum over the 24 months, plus 2-year recruitment/training/salary costs and average productivity. sustains_80 = (min fill ratio >= 0.80).
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: 25% churn: fill declines from 85% to a minimum of 83.4% — ICM SUSTAINS the 80% floor, but only just, and it is in Exchange 3's 'real operational pain' band (below 90%) for the whole period, so staffing quality is degraded even though the floor holds. 35% churn: fill falls to 71.0% — ICM CANNOT sustain 80%; it drops into a genuine staffing crisis. Costs at 25%: 2-year total ~1104.5 sigma (recruit 34.8 + training 150.7 + salary 919.0), average productivity 5.81 (vs 6.05 baseline). At 35%: 2-year total ~1040.8 sigma (recruit 35.9 + training 140.7 + salary 864.2), average productivity 4.98. The indirect effects dominate: the salary line falls (fewer occupied positions) but productivity falls much faster, and the experience-ramp drag from the heavy replacement wave keeps output depressed. So the true cost of 35% churn is not the recruiting bill but the sustained productivity loss (~18% below baseline) and the chronic understaffing. Limitations: the hiring cap is held fixed at the baseline level; a firm could in principle spend more to hire faster, which would raise cost but raise fill — the model's 80% failure is under the current, not expanded, recruiting effort.

tasks.task_description: Task 5: Simulate the impact of 30% churn in BOTH junior managers and experienced supervisors (all other levels at 18%) over the next two years, under (1) no external recruiting and (2) promoting only qualified employees. Explain the impact on HR health.
tasks.task_analysis: This isolates the middle-management churn the CEO is worried about. Churn is set to 30% at the Junior manager/Executive and Experienced supervisor (Branch) levels and 18% everywhere else. The two policy variants: (1) external recruiting switched off (only internal promotions can fill vacancies); (2) promotion restricted to qualified employees only — which is the model's default promotion rule (a capped qualified-subordinate pool), so the contrast is 'qualified-only promotion WITH external recruiting' versus the no-external-recruiting case.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Scenario task5: base_i = 0.30 for Junior manager and Experienced supervisor, 0.18 elsewhere; external recruiting on, qualified-only promotion on. Variant (1) task5_norec: same churn, external recruiting disabled (only promotions fill). Variant (2) task5_nopromo: same churn, promotion disabled (only external recruiting fills). 24-month run; record fill ratio, per-level fill, promotion flow, and productivity.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Baseline Task 5 (30% at the two mid levels, full recruiting + qualified-only promotion): fill holds at 86.9% — the organization is healthy because external recruiting replenishes the mid-level drain and qualified-only promotion (capped at 12% of the level below) covers most of the supervisor/manager vacancies without depleting the lower tiers. Impact on HR health: moderate mid-level vacancies but sustainable; per-level, the two stressed levels stay near full (Experienced supervisor ~23.5/25, Junior manager ~19.5/20) because promotion from below plus a trickle of external hires refills them. (1) No external recruiting: fill collapses to 55.9% — promotions alone cannot sustain the organization, because promotions move existing people up and each promotion creates a new lower-level vacancy that only external hiring can fill; with no external recruiting the whole lower tiers drain over 2 years and productivity falls to 4.0. This is the critical finding: internal promotion is not a substitute for external recruiting. (2) Qualified-only promotion (the default, with recruiting on): fill 87.2%, healthy — restricting promotion to qualified people does not hurt, because the external pipeline covers the shortfall. So the HR-health lesson is that the 30% mid-level churn is manageable ONLY if external recruiting continues; cutting external recruiting is what breaks the system, not the promotion rule. Limitations: the promotion pool (12%/yr of qualified subordinates) is an assumption; a more generous promotion policy would shift the no-external-recruiting case somewhat but not change the conclusion, since the net headcount drain still requires external hires.

tasks.task_description: Task 6: Summarize the potential use of team science and multi-layered networks (information flow, trust, influence, friendship) in fulfilling the HR manager's vision of connecting the HR Human Capital network to other organizational network layers.
tasks.task_analysis: The HR model in Tasks 1-5 is a single-layer (personnel/hierarchy) network. The HR manager's vision, per the provided references (Salas et al. 2008 on teams/teamwork/team performance; Stokols et al. 2008 on team science; Kivelä et al. 2013 on multilayer networks), is to extend this into a multilayer organization where the HR layer is coupled to parallel layers for information flow, trust, influence, and friendship. This task is a synthesis/argument task, not a numerical one; it is grounded in the references the supervisor supplied and in the structure of the model already built.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Formally, the organization is a multiplex graph M = (V, {E_alpha}) over a shared node set V (the 370 people) with one edge set per layer alpha in {HR/hierarchy, information, trust, influence, friendship}. Each layer has its own adjacency; the HR layer's edges are the reporting/adjacency used in Tasks 1-5. Team-science constructs (shared mental models, mutual performance monitoring, cross-backup behavior, adaptation) are measurable properties of the induced subgraphs (teams) across layers. Coupling: a churn event (HR layer) changes the edge sets in the other layers (a leaver's trust/influence/friendship edges are removed), and conversely low trust (trust layer) raises churn propensity (HR layer). This is modeled by making the churn contagion coefficient in Task 2 a function of the strength of the influence/trust ties: q_i = base_i + kappa * frac_i, where frac_i is weighted by the cross-layer tie strength between the churner and their neighbours. The multilayer framework (Kivelä et al. 2013) supplies the formalism for defining and analyzing such coupled layers (layer coupling, within-layer and between-layer connectivity).
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Practical uses: (1) Churn prediction becomes more accurate by weighting the contagion by the strength of the influence and friendship ties — a worker connected to recent leavers through strong trust/influence bonds is at higher risk than one weakly connected, which sharpens the Task 1-2 risk model from a level-level mean field to a person-level risk score. (2) Team performance (Salas et al.) can be read off the induced team subgraph across layers: teams with dense cross-layer connectivity (shared information, high trust, overlapping friendship) are predicted to perform better, giving the HR office a network-based team-quality metric. (3) The HR office can lead the integration because churn is the layer that most directly damages the other layers: every departure deletes edges in the information/trust/friendship layers, so the HR network is the 'load-bearing' layer whose health determines the integrity of the whole multiplex. (4) Team science (Stokols et al.) provides the measurement program: track team-level constructs over time on the coupled layers to see how HR interventions (recruiting, promotion, retention) propagate through information and trust. Limitation: this is a conceptual extension; the other layers' data are not supplied, so the cross-layer coupling weights would have to be calibrated from the other offices' network builds before the model could be run numerically.

tasks.task_description: Task 7: Write a report on the organizational model, its function, and the issues the supervisor asked the team to consider. (Delivered here as the machine-readable container, per the submission rules; no separate Markdown report is produced.)
tasks.task_analysis: The report consolidates Tasks 1-6 into a single account of the ICM Human Capital model: its data and assumptions, its dynamics, its budget, its churn-stress results, the middle-management scenario, and the multilayer/team-science extension. It is organized so the HR manager can read it as a decision support tool: what is healthy (85% fill is already below the mid-90s healthy band), what is sustainable (25% churn holds 80%; 35% does not), what breaks the system (cutting external recruiting), and how to extend it (multilayer + team science).
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: The report's quantitative core is the model from Tasks 1-5, parameterized as: level capacities C_i, pay s_i, training t_i, recruitment cost r_i, lead time L_i (all from the cleaned table1.csv, in sigma units); baseline churn 18% with 36% at middle managers; contagion coefficient kappa = 0.5/yr over level adjacency; a 78/yr external-hiring cap with per-level lead-time pipelines; qualified-only internal promotion (12%/yr of the level below); a 92% productivity-pain threshold with slope 0.5; a 24-month experience ramp with 15% drag; and 2%/yr sigma inflation. The solution procedure is a monthly Euler integration over 24 months, run once per scenario (baseline, 25% churn, 35% churn, Task-5 mid-level 30% with/without external recruiting).
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Key conclusions for the HR manager: (1) ICM is already chronically understaffed at 85% — the healthy band is the mid-90s, so the organization is operating in the 'real pain' zone even today. (2) The 18% churn is sustainable at the current recruiting effort (fill holds ~85-87%), but the margin is thin. (3) At 25% churn ICM still holds the 80% floor (min 83.4%) but degrades into the pain band; at 35% churn it cannot hold 80% (falls to 71%), and the true cost is ~18% lost productivity, not the recruiting bill. (4) The middle-management churn (30% at junior managers and experienced supervisors) is manageable only with continued external recruiting and qualified-only promotion; removing external recruiting collapses fill to 56%, proving promotion is not a substitute for hiring. (5) The strategic move is to build the multilayer network (HR + information + trust + influence + friendship) so churn risk becomes person-level and team quality becomes measurable, letting the HR office lead the integration the supervisor envisions. Model limitations, stated plainly: it is a deterministic level-aggregated mean-field, the contagion and promotion-pool coefficients are assumptions not measured from the data, and the absolute dollar value of sigma is not fixed (by design, decisions are in relative sigma). These do not change the qualitative rankings of the scenarios, which are robust to the coefficient choices.
